name: Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2511.20857, cs.CL/cs.AI). Submitted 25 Nov 2025 (v1), last revised 18 May 2026 (v2). Indexed by DBLP/OpenReview as CoRR 2025 (dblp:journals/corr/abs-2511-20857, OpenReview id iaAX2TFzRP); no peer-reviewed conference/journal venue confirmed at the time of writing.

code_url: https://github.com/zhaosnw/evo_mem (MIT License; full Evo-Memory benchmark + framework with ExpRAG, ReMem, ExpRecent and baselines ReAct, A-mem, Self-RAG, Mem0, LangMem, Dynamic Cheatsheet, AWM; includes the paper PDF and dataset download scripts). The paper states code and configurations will be released for reproducibility.
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/zhaosnw/evo_mem (16 stars / 4 forks as of mid-2026; last commit Dec 2025). No separate leaderboard page found.
task_domain: LLM-agent test-time learning across two task families: (1) single-turn reasoning and QA (multi-disciplinary MCQ MMLU-Pro, graduate science GPQA-Diamond, Olympiad math AIME-24/25, tool-use/API grounding ToolBench) and (2) multi-turn goal-oriented / embodied interactive decision-making (AlfWorld household, BabyAI navigation, ScienceWorld experimentation, PDDL symbolic planning). Spans QA, math, tool-use, planning, and embodied domains. This is a benchmark + framework paper (with two proposed methods ExpRAG and ReMem).
problem_setting: Streaming, interactive, single-agent test-time learning ('test-time evolution'). Static datasets are restructured into sequential task streams tau={(x1,y1),...,(xT,yT)}; at each step t the agent receives input x_t, retrieves from an evolving memory M_t, synthesizes a working context, produces an output y_hat_t, and updates memory M_{t+1}=U(M_t,m_t). The agent must accumulate and reuse experience across the stream WITHOUT updating model weights (memory is external; no gradient training). A correctness/feedback signal f_t is available (the ground-truth correctness of the task is used as feedback when constructing memory entries). Memory-augmented agents are formalized as a tuple (F, U, R, C): base LLM F, memory update pipeline U, retrieval module R, context construction C. Backbones are proprietary LLMs (Gemini-2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite/Pro; Claude 3.5-Haiku, 3.7-Sonnet) used inference-only via APIs. The benchmark unifies 10+ memory modules under one search-synthesize(predict)-evolve protocol.
what_is_retrieved: Prior task EXPERIENCES (structured experience text S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) encoding past task input, the agent's solution/trajectory, and correctness feedback), plus, depending on the memory module, distilled reasoning rationales/skills, procedural workflows (AWM), or aggregated 'cheatsheets' (Dynamic Cheatsheet). For multi-turn tasks, retrieved experiences include the goal, action-sequence trajectory, and success/failure label. The core unit emphasized by ExpRAG/ReMem is the task-level experience (problem + solution + correctness).
retrieval_grounding: GROWING / episodic self-written memory. The retrievable store starts effectively empty (cold start) and is populated online during the streaming evaluation from the agent's own past task experiences; memory is retrieved, integrated, and updated continuously during deployment. No static external corpus/KB/API store is the retrieval target (ToolBench APIs are a task, not the retrieval index). Hence grounding is a growing experience memory, not a static corpus.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k ranking objective. ExpRAG retrieves the Top-k experiences m_i in M_t by retrieval score phi(x_t, m_i); the unified configuration uses a fixed retrieval budget (default k=4) of most-similar memory items appended to the prompt in order of relevance. There is no minimal-complete-set or precision-driven variable-size objective; ReMem adds an adaptive prune/refine step over the retrieved set but the base retrieval is fixed top-k.
retrieval_unit: case (problem-solution experience): a structured experience text m_i = S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) (task input + predicted solution/trajectory + correctness feedback). For multi-turn tasks the unit is a full task trajectory (goal + action sequence + success/failure); for single-turn it is a (question, rationale/answer, correctness) experience. Other unified modules use their native units (AWM = workflow-routine; Dynamic Cheatsheet = aggregated cheatsheet text; Mem0 = memory fact items).
index_source: Growing memory, online / test-time-induced. The store is built incrementally during the streaming evaluation from the agent's own task experiences (append for retrieval-based memories; summarize/compress for long-term stores; replace for bounded stores). It is not offline-induced and not a fixed external corpus; each dataset is converted into a streaming task sequence over which memory evolves.
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index by default: all stored memory items are embedded with BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 and retrieved by top-k embedding similarity (cosine) against the current query. Unified modules contribute alternative organizations within the same framework: Mem0/MemOS use hierarchical/structured agent-level memory, AWM organizes reusable workflows, Dynamic Cheatsheet maintains an aggregated/curated cheatsheet; but the common retrieval substrate is a flat embedding index over memory items.
retriever_type: Dense (embedding-based) retriever using the off-the-shelf BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 encoder to index both queries and memory items, with top-k nearest-neighbor (cosine similarity) retrieval. ExpRecent uses recency-based retrieval instead of similarity. Some modules (Self-RAG, ReMem) add LLM-based reasoning on top to decide whether/what to retrieve, but the underlying retriever is dense embedding similarity.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf). The BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 retriever encoder is frozen and used as-is to ensure a consistent retrieval budget and fair comparison across all methods; there is no contrastive fine-tuning, LM-feedback training, RL, or downstream-effectiveness optimization of the retriever. Adaptive behaviors (Self-RAG reflection, ReMem Think/Refine) are prompt-driven LLM decisions layered on top of the same fixed retrieval pool, not a trained retrieval policy.
query_construction: Raw input query: the current task input/question x_t is encoded by the retriever and matched against stored memory embeddings. ReMem additionally uses LLM 'Think'/'Refine' reasoning to decide whether to retrieve and which retrieved experiences to keep or prune, and Self-RAG adaptively decides whether to retrieve, but the base query is the raw current input. No systematic sub-query decomposition or synthetic query expansion in the core pipeline.
query_granularity: Primarily task-level (one query per incoming task x_t at the start of the task). For multi-turn embodied tasks the retrieved experiences are injected into the task context and the agent then runs a multi-step loop; ReMem can perform additional Think/Refine memory operations within a step, but retrieval over experiences is keyed at the task level rather than per-environment-step. Effectively task-level with an adaptive intra-task refine layer for ReMem.
when_to_retrieve: Mostly one-shot per task for ExpRAG/ExpRecent (retrieve top-k experiences at the start of each task). ReMem and Self-RAG are adaptive: they introduce reasoning modules that decide whether to retrieve and what to retrieve, so retrieval can be triggered/refined adaptively within the agent loop. Overall the framework supports one-shot (ExpRAG) through adaptive (ReMem) retrieval.
retrieval_trigger_signal: ExpRAG/ExpRecent: fixed schedule (retrieve at the start of every task). ReMem: agent-initiated / reasoning-driven trigger - the agent chooses among {Think, Act, Refine} operations, and the Refine (and Think) steps perform meta-reasoning over memory deciding whether to exploit, prune, or reorganize retrieved experiences before acting (a step terminates once Act is selected). Self-RAG uses reflection-style decisions about whether to retrieve. No token-confidence or attention-entropy signal.
reranking: No dedicated cross-encoder/RRF reranking stage. Retrieved items are appended to the prompt ordered by embedding similarity (most to least similar). ReMem instead applies an LLM-driven Refine/Think-Prune operation that selects/prunes which retrieved experiences are kept (an interpretable LLM-based filtering rather than a learned reranker).
retrieved_context_refinement: For ExpRAG: minimal (similarity-ordered append, truncated to prompt budget). For ReMem: explicit Refine-Memory module performs meta-reasoning over retrieved memory - exploiting useful experiences, pruning noise (Think-Prune: remove unhelpful experiences by ID), and reorganizing M_t to better support reasoning and action; Dynamic Cheatsheet merges retrieved content into a short curated summary. So refinement ranges from none/truncation (ExpRAG) to active prune-and-reorganize distillation (ReMem).
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation (in-context learning). Retrieved experiences are inserted into a structured prompt (e.g., a 'RELEVANT EXPERIENCE FROM SIMILAR TASKS' section with goal/trajectory/correctness for multi-turn, or 'LOCAL EXPERIENCE MEMORY' rationales/skills for single-turn) and the base LLM conditions on them: y_hat_t = F(x_t, R_t). No weight updates or latent-token injection; memory is external and consumed via context. ReMem additionally lets the model reason about and update its own memory during problem solving.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-plan with an interleaved refine loop. ExpRAG performs one-shot retrieve-then-act in-context. ReMem expands the ReAct action space into {Think, Act, Refine}: the agent interleaves internal reasoning (Think), environment actions (Act), and memory meta-reasoning (Refine) within a Markov decision process where state s_t^n = (x_t, M_t, o_t^{1:n-1}); multiple Think/Refine rounds can occur before an Act terminates the step. Memory thus becomes an adaptive component woven into the act-think loop rather than static context. No explicit MCTS/tree search.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: ExpRAG: per-task / per-answer (retrieve once, then solve). ReMem: per-step within a rollout for multi-turn tasks (Think/Act/Refine operations interleaved across environment steps), and per-operation memory reasoning within a step. So interleaving granularity is per-task for the retrieval baseline and per-action/per-step (with intra-step memory refine) for ReMem.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured experience text / note: each memory entry is a templated experience S(x_i, y_hat_i, f_i) recording past task, solution/trajectory, and correctness, surfaced as free-text in the prompt (e.g., Goal / Trajectory / Correctness for multi-turn; rationale/domain/skill notes for single-turn). AWM contributes free-text workflows and Dynamic Cheatsheet a distilled cheatsheet; the proposed methods inject raw-to-lightly-distilled experience text, not executable programs or latent tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Spans raw-to-distilled. ExpRAG/ExpRecent retrieve near-raw task experiences/trajectories with correctness labels (single demonstration / raw trajectory level). ReMem operates over the same experiences but distills/prunes them via Refine into a more useful working memory. Unified baselines cover more abstract forms: AWM (reusable workflow routines), Dynamic Cheatsheet (distilled strategy aggregate). The paper finds explicit task-level (experience) utilization is both promising and underexplored.
noise_robustness_mechanism: ReMem's Refine-Memory module is the central noise-robustness mechanism: it actively prunes unhelpful/noisy experiences (Think-Prune by ID) and reorganizes memory, making it robust when both successful AND failed experiences are stored (Table 3) whereas baselines degrade under unfiltered failures. Keeping a small retrieval budget (default k=4, truncated to prompt length) and similarity-ordered injection also limits noise. Memory pruning analysis (Appendix B.2) shows higher pruning for diverse datasets (GPQA 36.8%) vs concentrated ones (AIME 17.5%/10.8%), evidencing selective discarding of domain-irrelevant experiences.
memory_type: episodic experience memory (with procedural/workflow variants among the unified modules). The proposed ExpRAG/ExpRecent/ReMem maintain a growing pool of episodic task experiences (trajectories + correctness); baselines instantiate skill/workflow memory (AWM), curated procedural cheatsheets (Dynamic Cheatsheet), and structured/hierarchical agent memory (Mem0, MemOS, LangMem). The framework abstracts all as evolving memory M_t.
write_back: Yes. After each task the agent constructs a new memory entry m_t = h(x_t, y_hat_t, f_t) capturing the experience and feedback, and updates memory via M_{t+1} = U(M_t, m_t). For ExpRAG, U is a direct append: M_{t+1} = M_t union {(x_t, y_hat_t, f_t)}. Different modules use append (retrieval-based), summarize/compress (long-term), or replace (bounded-capacity).
online_growth: Yes. Memory grows continuously during the streaming test-time deployment; the entire premise of 'test-time evolution' is that the store accumulates and evolves after every interaction across the task stream (starting from a cold start). Cumulative-accuracy curves (Appendix B.3) show ReMem surpassing the History baseline as more tasks accumulate.
write_back_trigger: Per-task (after every interaction), using the correctness feedback f_t. The agent writes a new experience entry after each completed task regardless of outcome (both successful and failed experiences can be stored, as analyzed in RQ4/Table 3). ReMem additionally performs reflective Refine operations that reorganize/prune existing memory during problem solving, so writing/updating is per-task with reflective in-loop refinement.
failure_experience_usage: Success + failure stored, with selective refinement. Experiences carry a correctness label (success/failure), and RQ4 (Table 3) explicitly evaluates storing BOTH successful and failed experiences on AlfWorld/ScienceWorld: naive baselines degrade under unfiltered failures (noise), while ReMem stays robust by actively refining/pruning stored experiences, achieving the best success/progress. The paper motivates future work on failure-aware memory evolution. So failures are retained and used, but require ReMem-style filtering to be beneficial.
memory_evolution_update: Depends on module: append-only (ExpRAG direct union), summarization/compression (long-term stores), or replacement (bounded-capacity stores). ReMem adds delta-update + forget-prune + reorganize: its Refine operation prunes noisy entries (Think-Prune by ID) and reorganizes M_t over time. Reported memory pruning rates vary by dataset (e.g., GPQA 36.8% pruned vs AIME 10.8%-17.5%), demonstrating active forgetting/curation rather than pure append.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No (not a trained/RL retrieval policy). Retrieval is fixed top-k embedding similarity over a frozen bge-base encoder. ReMem's decision to retrieve/refine/prune is an LLM-prompted (in-context) meta-reasoning policy framed as a Markov decision process, but it is NOT optimized via RL or value learning - the LLM weights are not updated. So memory control is reasoning-driven but not a learned/parameter-optimized policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No. Single-agent private memory: each agent maintains and evolves its own memory across its task stream. The benchmark UNIFIES many memory frameworks under one protocol for comparison, but memory/experience is not shared across multiple agents or across heterogeneous frameworks at run time.
benchmarks: Single-turn: MMLU-Pro (Engineering 969q, Economics 844q, Philosophy 499q domains used; ~12K total across 14 areas), GPQA-Diamond (198 graduate-level science MCQ), AIME-24 and AIME-25 (30 Olympiad math problems each, exact-match), ToolBench/Gorilla (750 tool-use/API-grounding tasks). Multi-turn embodied/interactive: AlfWorld (134 text household tasks), BabyAI (112 grid navigation/manipulation tasks), ScienceWorld (90 interactive science tasks), PDDL (60 symbolic planning problems). 10 datasets total.
benchmark_family: Mixed: QA / multi-disciplinary reasoning (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond), math (AIME-24/25), tool (ToolBench), and embodied/interactive decision-making (AlfWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld - embodied; PDDL - symbolic planning). No LoCoMo/LongMemEval-style conversational-memory benchmarks (the paper positions itself against those static-recall settings) and no D4RL decision-RL.
baselines: Grouped into four families. (1) Agent pipelines without procedural memory: ReAct, A-mem (Amem); also a 'Baseline' (zero-shot) and 'History' (raw history context). (2) Adaptive agentic memory: Self-RAG (SelfRAG), MemOS, Mem0, LangMem. (3) Procedural-memory agents: Dynamic Cheatsheet (DC-Cu = Cumulative/curated, DC-RS = Retrieval-Synthesis), Agent Workflow Memory (AWM). (4) Proposed evolving-memory framework: ExpRecent, ExpRAG, ReMem. MemoryBank/MemoryGPT excluded (factual recall only); MemOS and LangMem excluded from multi-turn embodied evaluation as incompatible.
key_metrics: Single-turn: Exact Match (AIME, GPQA, MMLU-Pro) and API/Accuracy for ToolBench (reported as API/Acc., e.g., 0.85/0.71), plus an average. Multi-turn: Success rate (S) and Progress rate (P) per environment, plus averages. Also Step efficiency (average steps to complete a task; lower is better), Sequence robustness (consistency across Easy->Hard vs Hard->Easy orderings), and cumulative accuracy/success over the task stream. Pearson correlation r used to relate ReMem gains to within-dataset task similarity.
headline_result: Across single-turn and multi-turn tasks, evolving-memory methods (ExpRAG, ReMem) consistently outperform baselines; gains are largest in multi-turn settings. On multi-turn (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) ReMem reaches average S/P = 0.78/0.91 vs Baseline 0.24/0.52 and ReAct 0.57/0.79, with AlfWorld 0.92/0.96, BabyAI 0.73/0.83, PDDL 0.83/0.95, ScienceWorld 0.62/0.89. On Gemini-2.5-Flash multi-turn, ReMem averages 0.50/0.64 vs Baseline 0.27/0.46. On single-turn (Gemini-2.5-Flash) ReMem achieves 0.65 average exact match with ToolBench API/Acc 0.85/0.71, the best in its column. ReMem also cuts steps substantially (e.g., AlfWorld 22.6 -> 11.5 steps).
ablations: (1) RQ2 memory-improvement vs task similarity (Fig.3): ReMem's gain over History correlates with within-dataset task similarity (Pearson r=0.717 Gemini-2.5-Flash, r=0.563 Claude-3.7-Sonnet); high-similarity datasets (PDDL, AlfWorld) gain most, diverse ones (AIME-25, GPQA) gain least. (2) RQ3 sequence difficulty (Table 2): evolving-memory robust to Easy->Hard vs Hard->Easy ordering; ReMem reaches up to 0.94/0.97 (Hard->Easy), and harder-task experiences transfer better. (3) RQ4 feedback / success+failure storage (Table 3): baselines degrade under unfiltered failures; ReMem stays robust via refinement (Claude AlfWorld 0.92/0.96, ScienceWorld 0.69/0.91). (4) Step efficiency (Fig.4): ReMem largest, most stable step reductions. (5) Memory pruning rates (Fig.5/App B.2): GPQA 36.8% pruned vs AIME 10.8%-17.5%. (6) Cross-model (App B.1, Tables 4-5): trends hold across Gemini-2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite/Pro and Claude-3.5-Haiku/3.7-Sonnet; smaller models benefit most. (7) Cumulative accuracy curves (App B.3): ReMem surpasses History as tasks accumulate.
evaluation_decoupling: No. Only end-to-end task metrics (exact match, success/progress rate, API accuracy) plus efficiency (steps), robustness, and cumulative accuracy are reported. No intrinsic retrieval metrics (Recall@k / nDCG / retrieval completeness) are reported separately; the closest decoupled memory-quality signal is the memory pruning-rate analysis and the task-similarity correlation.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Mixed. Outcome metrics (exact match, success rate, API accuracy) are primary, but the framework explicitly adds process/efficiency signals: Progress rate (partial completion in multi-turn), Step efficiency (number of steps), Sequence robustness (cross-ordering consistency), cumulative accuracy/success over the stream, and memory pruning/selectivity analysis. So intermediate process quality (progress, steps, adaptation curves) is evaluated alongside final outcome.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Reported via step efficiency and qualitative compute notes. Evolving-memory methods need fewer steps to complete multi-turn tasks; ReMem gives the largest, most stable reductions (e.g., AlfWorld 22.6 -> 11.5 steps; Fig.4). Smaller/lightweight LLMs benefit most from test-time refinement (App B.1). A fixed retrieval budget (default k=4, prompt-length truncation) is enforced for fair comparison. Total API compute cost for the study was 'on the order of tens of thousands of US dollars' (App G.1); exact per-method token/latency costs are not tabulated.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-k, budget-capped. Default top-k = 4 most-relevant memory items retrieved per task via bge-base similarity, appended in similarity order and truncated so retrieved texts + task input fit within the same prompt-length constraint across all methods (ensuring a consistent retrieval budget). ReMem may further prune the retrieved set adaptively. Memory store size configurable (e.g., memory_size 1000 in the released config).
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (this is a benchmark/framework paper, not a survey). It does, however, organize evaluated methods along four families: (1) agent pipelines without procedural memory, (2) adaptive agentic memory, (3) procedural-memory agents, (4) the proposed evolving-memory framework; and evaluates along four dimensions: answer accuracy, success rate, step efficiency, sequence robustness.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Construction: Evo-Memory TRANSFORMS existing static datasets into streaming task sequences tau={(x1,y1),...,(xT,yT)} with a unified, fixed task ordering per dataset, so earlier tasks supply information/strategies for later ones; evaluated under the unified search-synthesize-evolve loop with correctness as feedback. Size: 10 datasets - single-turn (MMLU-Pro using Eng 969q/Eco 844q/Philo 499q domains, GPQA-Diamond 198q, AIME-24 30q, AIME-25 30q, ToolBench 750 tasks) and multi-turn (AlfWorld 134, BabyAI 112, ScienceWorld 90, PDDL 60). Answers verifiable via exact match (math/QA), API/execution-based accuracy (ToolBench), and success/progress rates (embodied). Difficulty signaled by low baseline scores (e.g., AIME exact match ~0.13-0.47; multi-turn baseline averages ~0.24-0.27 success) vs ReMem reaching 0.78 avg success on Claude-3.7-Sonnet multi-turn. 10+ memory modules unified and implemented.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (top-k similarity / recency retrieval of past experiences), Reuse: yes (retrieved experiences injected as in-context exemplars to solve the current task), Revise: yes (ReMem's Refine/Think-Prune meta-reasoning revises and reorganizes retrieved/stored experiences; ExpRAG reuses without per-case adaptation), Retain: yes (new experience m_t=h(x_t,y_hat_t,f_t) appended/updated via U after each task)]. The framework implements all four CBR phases (most fully in ReMem), though not framed as CBR.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The paper frames itself as 'self-evolving memory', 'test-time learning/evolution', and 'experience reuse' for LLM agents; it does NOT cite Aamodt & Plaza or Kolodner or use the term 'case-based reasoning'. It realizes CBR-like Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain mechanisms under memory/experience-learning terminology.
tool_document_engineering: N/A. ToolBench is used as a task (API selection/configuration), not as a retrievable tool index with engineered tool descriptions. Memory items are task experiences, not tool docstrings, so no tool-document engineering (synthetic-query augmentation, weighted-field embeddings, etc.).
index_content_separation: Partial. Multi-turn experiences are stored with lightweight identifiers (goal + correctness label) alongside heavier trajectory content, and ReMem references experiences by ID for pruning (Think-Prune: <IDs>). However there is no formal progressive-disclosure / index-then-load-content mechanism; retrieved experiences are injected as whole items (truncated to the prompt budget).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A. No live external tool registry or integration protocol (MCP/RapidAPI/RESTful/function-calling) is synchronized; the memory store is an internally-managed growing pool of experiences. LLM access is via official vendor SDKs/APIs, but that is not a tool-index protocol.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; tools are not the retrieval unit).
adaptation_mechanism: ExpRAG: verbatim in-context exemplar reuse (retrieved experiences used as ICL examples without per-case editing). ReMem: LLM-prompted adaptation + meta-reasoning - the Think/Refine operations exploit useful experiences, prune noise, and reorganize memory before/while acting, effectively revising the working memory rather than copy-editing a single retrieved solution; feedback (correctness) informs what is retained. No RL reuse-finetuning or latent adaptation.
builds_on: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023) as the reasoning-acting backbone that ReMem extends with a Refine/memory-reasoning action; retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al. 2020) and Self-RAG (Asai et al. 2024) for adaptive retrieval; unified memory baselines A-mem (Xu et al. 2025), Mem0, MemOS (Li et al. 2025), LangMem, Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al. 2025), and Agent Workflow Memory / AWM (Wang et al. 2024); BAAI bge-base-en-v1.5 (Chen et al. 2024) retriever. Benchmark datasets: MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, AIME-24/25, ToolBench/Gorilla, AlfWorld, BabyAI, ScienceWorld, PDDLbench. Prior streaming/lifelong benchmarks StreamBench (Wu et al. 2024) and LifelongAgentBench (Zheng et al. 2025) are the closest predecessors it extends.
contrasts_with: Static conversational-memory benchmarks and methods that test recall rather than experience reuse (LongMemEval, LoCoMo-style evaluations, Maharana et al. 2024; MemoryBank/MemoryGPT - excluded as factual-recall only). Also contrasts with StreamBench (sequential learning but mainly factual retention, no trajectory reuse) and LifelongAgentBench (retention without modeling memory structure/updates). Within methods, it positions ExpRAG/ReMem against procedural-only (AWM, Dynamic Cheatsheet) and adaptive-retrieval-only (Self-RAG, Mem0, MemOS, LangMem) memories, arguing for tightly integrating reasoning + action + memory refinement (test-time evolution).
lineage: Group F (decision/memory/RL - self-evolving agent memory & test-time learning). A 2025-2026 streaming BENCHMARK + framework that operationalizes 'test-time evolution', advancing the lifelong/streaming-agent line (StreamBench, LifelongAgentBench) and the self-evolving agent-memory line (ExpeL/Synapse/AWM/Reflexion/ReasoningBank/Dynamic Cheatsheet). Distinctive contributions: (a) restructuring static datasets into streaming task streams to test experience reuse vs conversational recall; (b) a unified (F,U,R,C) search-synthesize-evolve formulation unifying 10+ memory modules; (c) ExpRAG (simple but strong task-level experience-retrieval baseline) and ReMem (an action-think-memory-refine pipeline extending ReAct with explicit memory reasoning).
